claims.text: The as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy has a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state.
A combined high-pressure and high-temperature treatment can convert the starting Mg-containing lightweight alloy into a single-phase solid solution.
The treatment temperature should be above 600 K.
High pressure is required to induce the proposed phase conversion.
Exposure for a sufficient time will permit the phase transformation.
High pressure decreases atomic-size and electronegativity differences between the solute elements and the host alloy.
A synergistic high-entropy effect produced by high temperature and high pressure promotes formation of the single-phase solid solution.
Conversion of intermetallic or brittle phases into a single-phase solid solution overcomes limitations associated with intermetallic formation.
The high-pressure and high-temperature treatment will improve room-temperature compressive behavior relative to the as-processed alloy.
The treatment will enhance corrosion resistance relative to the as-processed alloy.
The treatment will increase resistance to high-temperature oxidation relative to the as-processed alloy.
The relevant treatment or operating boundary is below 700 °C.
The pressure should remain below the critical pressure for phase transformation.
Limiting high-temperature exposure time can prevent excessive oxidation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis requires pressure sufficient to produce a phase transformation into a single-phase solid solution, but its stated boundary requires pressure to remain below the critical pressure for that transformation.
